newsitem.title: USA: Scientists celebrate Pathfinder's first week on Mars.
newsitem.headline: Scientists celebrate Pathfinder's first week on Mars.

text.p: Space scientists on Friday celebrated the first week on Mars of their Pathfinder spacecraft and the star of the show, a little buggy named Sojourner.
"This really has been a fantastic week, beyond our wildest dreams," said Project Scientist Matthew Golombek, a NASA geologist in charge of the Mars Pathfinder's scientific mission.
The Pathfinder lander hit the surface of the Red Planet with a thump last Friday in a carefully planned patriotic landing to coincide with America's Fourth of July Independence Day holiday.
Since then it has thrilled scientists and the public alike by providing a wealth of scientific information and stunning pictures sent back by the rover and it's "mother ship," the landing craft.

The Pathfinder has amassed a number of space firsts. It was first to deploy a parachute at supersonic speeds of 1,000 miles per hour (1,609 km per hour), first to use airbags to cushion its landing and to use a self-righting craft that signalled back to Earth it had arrived just three minutes after touch-down.
In the past week the rover has analysed a Martian rock that showed the Red Planet to be a solar twin of Earth because of its almost identical similarity to rocks on our own planet.

Pictures taken on the lander by a three-dimensional camera provided proof that there was water on Mars, and possibly a much warmer atmosphere. These are two of the vital ingredients to promoting life on the planet.
Scientists have long questioned whether life exists on Mars and there is hope that the Pathfinder and its successors may provide the answer.

But there have been some glitches during the mission. Initially, the rover's computer refused to talk to the computer aboard the lander craft, through which all communications to the Sojourner were to be sent. But that was solved by the crew at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena within 48 hours.

Then on Thursday, the rover crashed into a rock four times its size. But the microwave-size buggy sustained no damage, "and as far as we know Jack Morrison's (driver's) license is still valid," Mission Manager Richard Cook quipped in a reference to the Earth-bound controller of the rover.
The rover hit the rock, named "Yogi" by space scientists, as it was backing up and manoeuvring itself to position its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer against a flat surface.

Justin Maki, a science manager on the Pathfinder team, showed journalists a "movie" of the collision made up of several still frames. "It (the rover) drove too far. It was a little too enthusiastic," he said.
The incident delayed a survey of "Yogi," the second in a series of rocks targeted by engineers for analysis by Sojourner.
The little buggy, which is just one foot (0.3 meters) high by two feet (0.6 meters) long and 1.5 ft. (0.45 meters) wide, was due to complete its survey of "Yogi" on Friday.

The science team at Pasadena said "Yogi" was of particular interest because it appeared to be of a different composition to the first rock analysed, dubbed "Barnacle Bill" because of its crusty, pock-marked surface.
That analysis showed "Barnacle Bill" to have characteristics of being formed by volcanic activity, very much like rocks on Earth.
